README.AYUSH Medical Tourism Platform - Starter: Compiled 2 Nov 2026 from web research. Starter data only: verify every entry directly with the institution before publishing.
Institutions - one row per institution across all five systems (Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha, Homeopathy), with type, credentials, programmes and source. Use the System column to filter.
Price Points - individual price observations with currency, unit and duration, so you can filter and compare.
Yellow cells (Verification Status, Last Verified, Notes) are for you to fill in as you confirm each entry.
'Verified in research' = a source in this research states it. 'Needs verification' = from general knowledge or a self-published page.
Prices are indicative, taken from aggregator/booking sites and older reports. They often exclude medicines and consultations. Confirm via quote.
Ayurveda credential check: NABH publishes its accredited AYUSH hospital list with validity dates (e.g. AVS Kochi certificate valid to 12 Dec 2026).
Yoga has no hospital-style accreditation: use Yoga Alliance registration (YTT schools) and government affiliation instead.

Unani, Siddha and Homeopathy: coverage is mainly government national institutes (public rates, limited tourist marketing) plus Dr Batra's chain. Foreign-patient tariffs were not published; request quotes.
Visa note: India has a dedicated AYUSH visa (AY-1 patient, AY-2 attendant; e-AYUSH M3/M4 for e-Visa). Confirm current rules on official sites.
Added: Treatment Guide - plain-English explanation of each therapy (what it is, what happens, duration, traditional benefits, cautions, evidence note) across all five systems plus naturopathy.

Added: Safety Notes - key safety and wording guidance for your platform. Treatment descriptions are general information, not medical advice; have a qualified AYUSH or medical professional review them before publishing.
Benefit statements are phrased as 'traditionally used for' because evidence varies and many therapies are not proven by modern clinical trials.

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): A full cleansing-and-reset programme. Ayurveda holds that undigested waste ('ama') and imbalance in three body energies ('doshas': Vata = movement, Pitta = heat/digestion, Kapha = structure/moisture) build up and cause illness. Panchakarma tries to remove that build-up. It runs in three stages: preparation, main cleansing, then recovery.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Doctor consultation and personal plan; daily oil massage and steam; one or more main cleansing procedures (see Vamana, Virechana, Basti, Nasya, Raktamokshana); then a gentle diet and rest. Meals are light and mostly vegetarian; alcohol and heavy activity are avoided.
Treatment Guide.Typical duration: 7-28 days (14-21 days is typical for a full programme)
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Stress, digestive problems, joint and skin conditions, lifestyle-related conditions, general rejuvenation
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Pregnancy, very weak or elderly people, serious heart/kidney/liver disease, active infection or acute illness need clear medical approval. Procedures like induced vomiting and purgation must be doctor-supervised.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Limited / mixed evidence; small studies report benefits, results vary

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Oil therapy that prepares the body for cleansing. Medicated ghee or oil is drunk in slowly increasing doses (internal) and/or massaged onto the body (external).
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: For about 3-7 days you take a measured daily dose of medicated ghee on an empty stomach, along with oil massage. You may feel oily or sluggish; this is expected.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Loosening 'toxins' before cleansing; softening dry skin and joints
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Not suitable for some digestive, liver or high-cholesterol conditions without medical advice.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Whole-body or local sweating using herbal steam or heated herbal poultices, usually right after oil massage.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: You sit or lie in a steam chamber with your head outside, or have heated herbal bundles applied. Lasts about 10-20 minutes.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Stiffness, muscle and joint pain, colds, relaxation
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Heart disease, high blood pressure, pregnancy, fever, skin infection, reduced skin sensation (e.g. diabetes) - risk of burns or fainting.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Medically supervised induced vomiting, traditionally believed to clear excess Kapha (mucus-type) from the chest and stomach.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: After several days of oil therapy and steam, you drink herbal preparations in the morning and vomit under doctor supervision, then rest on a strict light diet.
Treatment Guide.Typical duration: 1 day, plus several days of preparation and recovery
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Traditionally for asthma, recurring colds, sinus problems, some skin conditions, obesity
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Not for pregnancy, heart disease, high blood pressure, ulcers, children, the elderly or weak. Must be doctor-supervised; risks include dehydration.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Limited / mixed evidence; small studies report benefits, results vary

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): A herbal laxative treatment under supervision, traditionally believed to clear excess Pitta (heat/digestion) from the liver and gut.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: After preparation days, you take a herbal laxative and have several bowel movements through the day under supervision, followed by a light diet.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Traditionally for skin problems, digestive and liver complaints, acidity, some metabolic conditions
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Pregnancy, severe weakness, rectal bleeding, acute diarrhoea. Risk of dehydration; medical supervision required.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Limited / mixed evidence; small studies report benefits, results vary

Treatment Guide.Also known as / meaning: Vasti; Niruha (herbal decoction) and Anuvasana (oil) types
Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Herbal decoctions or oils given as an enema. Ayurveda considers Basti the most important Panchakarma therapy, especially for Vata (movement) disorders.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: You lie on your side while a practitioner gives a measured medicated enema; you then rest. A course often uses several sessions across 8-16 days.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Traditionally for joint pain and arthritis, back pain, constipation, nerve and neurological conditions
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Rectal bleeding, severe diarrhoea, pregnancy, acute illness. Should be done by trained practitioners.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Limited / mixed evidence; small studies report benefits, results vary

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Herbal oil, powder or ghee drops placed in the nostrils to clear the head and sinuses.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: After a face massage and steam, you lie back and a few drops go into each nostril; you rest briefly afterwards.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Sinus congestion, headaches, migraine, stress, sleep problems
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Avoid during pregnancy, heavy cold with fever, or just after meals or bathing; follow doctor's instructions.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Limited / mixed evidence; small studies report benefits, results vary

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Removal of a small amount of blood, traditionally by medical leeches or small controlled cuts, to treat 'impure blood' conditions. Less common today than other Panchakarma steps.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Leeches are applied to a small area for some minutes or a small amount of blood is drawn by a trained practitioner; the area is then dressed.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Traditionally for skin conditions, localised joint inflammation, varicose problems
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Bleeding disorders, anaemia, blood thinners, pregnancy, low immunity. Insist on sterile, single-use equipment and fresh leeches used once.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Some studies on leech therapy for knee osteoarthritis; otherwise limited

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): A rhythmic massage with warm herbal oil, usually by one or two therapists. The most commonly offered Ayurvedic therapy.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: You lie on a wooden table while warm oil is applied across the whole body with long strokes; often followed by steam and a bath.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Relaxation, stress relief, muscle stiffness, better sleep, skin nourishment
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Skin infections, fever, just after meals, some skin allergies - ask about oil ingredients.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Relaxation benefits are well accepted; specific health claims limited

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): A continuous stream of warm oil (or herbal liquid) poured slowly over the forehead.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: You lie down while a thin stream of warm oil flows over your forehead for about 30-45 minutes.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Stress, anxiety, insomnia, headaches, mental fatigue
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Head injury, fever, sinus infection, some scalp conditions; avoid if you are unwell with a cold.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Some small studies on relaxation and sleep; limited

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Warm medicated oil is squeezed from cloth pouches over your body while therapists massage in rhythm. Often called the 'king of treatments' in Kerala.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Two to four therapists pour and massage warm oil over the body simultaneously for about 45-60 minutes.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Joint pain, arthritis, muscle weakness, nerve and neurological problems, stress
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Fever, acute inflammation, heart conditions, pregnancy; heat can cause discomfort for some.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Cloth bundles filled with cooked medicinal rice (Njavara) in milk and herbs are dipped in warm liquid and massaged over the body.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Therapists massage you with warm rice-filled bundles for about 45-60 minutes.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Muscle wasting and weakness, joint stiffness, nerve conditions, skin nourishment
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Fever, acute infections, skin allergies; check with doctor in pregnancy.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Heated bundles of herbal leaves (Elakizhi) or herbal powders (Podikizhi) are pressed over the body.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Warm bundles are dabbed and rubbed over sore areas or the whole body.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Joint and muscle pain, stiffness, sprains, back pain
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Skin injuries or infections, fever, heat intolerance.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): A deep, upward-stroking massage with herbal powder, traditionally believed to reduce fat and tone the body.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: A therapist massages dry herbal powder against the direction of hair growth for about 30-45 minutes.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Weight management, cellulite, skin tone, sluggishness
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Sensitive or broken skin, bleeding disorders; may be too vigorous for some.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Warm medicated oil is held in a leather or cloth cap placed on the head.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: A cap is fitted to the head and filled with warm oil for 30-45 minutes.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Chronic headache, facial nerve conditions, insomnia, hair and scalp issues
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Head injury, fever, acute infection.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): A dam of dough is built around the eye and filled with warm medicated ghee, which you keep your eyes open in for a few minutes.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: You lie down while ghee is poured into the dough ring around each eye and blink in it for 5-20 minutes.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Eye strain, dry eyes, screen-related fatigue
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Eye infection, recent eye surgery, fever. Do not use for eye disease without an eye specialist's input.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Warm medicated oil is held in a ring of dough on the lower back, knee or neck.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: A dough ring is placed on the sore area and filled with warm oil, which is kept warm for 30-45 minutes.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Back pain, sciatica, knee pain, neck stiffness, spondylosis
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Skin infections, fever, acute injury; no treatment replaces medical assessment for serious pain, numbness or weakness.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Some studies on back and knee pain; quality varies

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Like Shirodhara, but with medicated buttermilk poured over the forehead.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: A stream of herbal buttermilk flows over the forehead for 30-45 minutes.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Stress, insomnia, scalp conditions, some skin conditions
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Cold, sinus infection, fever.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Gentle pressure or massage on special points of the body (similar in idea to acupressure) to relieve pain and release tension.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: A practitioner applies light pressure and oil on key points for pain relief or relaxation.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Pain, stress, neck and back stiffness, injury recovery
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Fractures, open wounds, acute injury, pregnancy (avoid certain points).
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): A programme of herbal tonics, diet and lifestyle intended to build strength and immunity and slow ageing. Often done after Panchakarma.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Your doctor prescribes herbal tonics, diet and routines, sometimes with a short resident stay.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Fatigue, low immunity, recovery from illness, general vitality
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Herbal tonics can interact with medicines; avoid mineral/metal preparations unless from a trusted, tested source (see Safety Notes).
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.Treatment: Prakriti & Nadi Pariksha (constitution and pulse assessment)
Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): The Ayurvedic consultation. The doctor assesses your body type ('prakriti'), current imbalances, digestion and pulse to design your plan.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: A long consultation with questions on diet, sleep, bowel habits and stress; pulse, tongue and body examination.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Used to personalise treatment
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Not a substitute for modern diagnostic tests for serious symptoms.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Diagnosis methods are traditional; not validated by modern medicine

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): A medicated surgical thread used to treat anal fistula and piles. One of the few Ayurvedic procedures with formal clinical use in a surgical context.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: A doctor ties a herbal-coated thread around the fistula or pile; it is tightened at intervals over weeks.
Treatment Guide.Typical duration: Procedure is brief; treatment runs over weeks
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Anal fistula, piles (haemorrhoids)
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Needs assessment by a qualified Ayurvedic surgeon or a modern surgeon.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Some clinical studies; used in Indian government hospitals

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Meal and daily routine advice matched to your constitution and condition, such as warm cooked food and regular timing.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Meals provided at the centre are planned by the doctor; you also get guidance for home.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Digestion, weight, general health maintenance
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Follow doctor's advice if you have diabetes, allergies or take regular medicines.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: General healthy-diet benefits are accepted; Ayurveda-specific claims limited

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Physical postures held for a period, combining stretching, strength and balance with controlled breathing.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Guided classes from gentle to vigorous; therapy centres tailor poses to a condition.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Flexibility, strength, back and joint pain, stress, general fitness
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Recent injury, pregnancy, uncontrolled blood pressure, glaucoma, and some spinal conditions need modified poses.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Reasonable evidence for low back pain and stress; benefits depend on style and practice

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Controlled breathing exercises such as alternate-nostril breathing.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Seated, guided breath patterns for 10-30 minutes.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Stress, focus, sleep, mild anxiety
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Avoid forceful breath-holding with heart disease, high blood pressure, pregnancy, or lung conditions.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Some evidence for stress and blood pressure; quality varies

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Training the mind to stay focused or aware, often through sitting practices.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Guided or silent sitting meditation; sometimes retreats of several days.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Stress, focus, emotional balance
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Intensive retreats can be hard for people with severe depression, trauma or psychosis; seek advice first.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Evidence for stress and anxiety; varies by technique

Treatment Guide.Also known as / meaning: Six cleansing techniques (e.g. Neti, Kapalabhati, Dhauti)
Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Traditional cleansing practices: nasal rinsing (Jala Neti), rapid breathing (Kapalabhati), stomach washing and others.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: A teacher demonstrates; Neti uses a small pot with saltwater flowed through the nose.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Sinus congestion, respiratory health, digestion
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Advanced kriyas (e.g. Dhauti, Basti) only under an experienced teacher; Neti must use clean, boiled or distilled water.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Some evidence for nasal saline rinsing; other kriyas limited

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): A guided lying-down relaxation that leads you through body awareness and breath.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: You lie down and follow a voice for 20-45 minutes.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Stress, insomnia, tension
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Generally safe; discuss with doctor if you have severe mental-health conditions.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Some small studies on stress and sleep

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Yoga tailored to a health condition by a trained therapist, often combining postures, breathing and relaxation.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: An assessment followed by a personalised daily routine, sometimes residential over 1-4 weeks.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Back pain, stress, hypertension, diabetes support, rehabilitation
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Not a replacement for medical treatment; keep taking prescribed medicines unless your doctor advises otherwise.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Reasonable evidence for some conditions (e.g. back pain, stress)

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Residential courses that train you to teach yoga; common durations are 100, 200, 300 and 500 hours.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Daily practice, philosophy, anatomy and teaching methodology in a residential setting; Yoga Alliance registration is common.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Personal practice, deepening knowledge, becoming a teacher
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Physically demanding; read the schedule carefully.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Not a medical treatment

Treatment Guide.Treatment: Yoga styles on offer (Hatha, Ashtanga, Iyengar, Vinyasa)
Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Hatha: slow, foundational. Ashtanga: fixed, vigorous sequence (Mysore). Iyengar: precise alignment, uses props. Vinyasa: flowing movement with breath.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Choose by fitness and goal; many places offer beginner levels.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Matches different fitness and interest levels
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Choose gentler styles if you are unfit, older or injured.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: N/A

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Using water in different forms and temperatures: hip baths, steam, spinal baths, wraps.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Short sessions in baths or showers; temperatures are controlled by the therapist.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Pain relief, circulation, relaxation, digestion
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Heart disease, severe high blood pressure, pregnancy, skin infections, and sensitivity to heat or cold need advice.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Some evidence for certain pain and relaxation uses; varies

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Cool wet mud packs applied to the body, belly, head or eyes.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Mud pack is applied for 20-30 minutes then rinsed.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Skin conditions, constipation, headache, heat relief
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Open wounds, skin infection, extreme cold sensitivity.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.Also known as / meaning: Supervised fasting, juice and raw-food diets
Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Planned short fasts, juice diets or raw-food days to rest digestion.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: A supervised diet plan, often combined with enemas, massages or yoga.
Treatment Guide.Typical duration: 1-3 days of fasting; longer diet programmes
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Weight loss, digestive rest, lifestyle diseases
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Diabetes, pregnancy, eating disorders, underweight people, and people on regular medicines must get medical advice; fasting can be harmful.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Mixed; some risks

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Massage and pressure on specific points to relieve tension.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Therapist applies massage or pressure for 30-60 minutes.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Muscle tension, pain, relaxation
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Injuries, fractures, bleeding disorders, pregnancy.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Unani's umbrella term for non-drug therapies such as cupping, massage, steam, bloodletting and exercise, used to expel harmful matter and restore balance of the four humours.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: A practitioner combines selected therapies in a plan; NIUM Bangalore has a dedicated Regimental Therapy Centre.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Musculoskeletal pain, skin conditions, chronic disorders
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Techniques that involve blood or heat need trained practitioners and strict hygiene.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Limited / mixed evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Cups are placed on the skin to create suction. Dry cupping only draws the skin up; wet cupping also makes tiny cuts to draw out a little blood.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Cups are placed on the back, shoulders or other areas for 5-15 minutes. Wet cupping adds light skin incisions.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Back and neck pain, muscle tension, headaches
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Blood thinners, bleeding disorders, anaemia, skin infections, pregnancy. Wet cupping needs sterile single-use equipment due to infection risk.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Some studies on pain; quality varies

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): A small amount of blood is drawn from a vein by a trained practitioner, based on the idea of removing excess blood.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Done in a clinic by a doctor with sterile equipment; the area is then dressed.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Traditionally for high blood pressure and some skin and inflammatory conditions
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Anaemia, low blood pressure, bleeding disorders, blood thinners, weakness; modern medicine would use other approaches for hypertension.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Therapeutic massage with medicated oils to relax muscles and improve circulation.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: A therapist massages with oils for 30-60 minutes.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Muscle stiffness, pain, relaxation
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Skin infections, fever, acute injury.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Relaxation benefits accepted; others limited

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): A heated steam room session, sometimes followed by massage.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: You sit in warm steam for 10-20 minutes, then cool down and rest.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Relaxation, skin, congestion, muscle ache
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Heart disease, high blood pressure, pregnancy, dehydration risk.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Medical leeches applied to the skin to draw out a small amount of blood.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Leeches are placed on the affected area for 20-40 minutes under supervision.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Skin conditions, joint pain, localised swelling
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Bleeding disorders, anaemia, blood thinners; use fresh single-use leeches.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Some studies on knee osteoarthritis pain; limited otherwise

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Medicated enema used for cleansing the colon, similar in idea to Ayurvedic Basti.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: A practitioner administers a herbal enema; you rest afterwards.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Constipation, digestive issues, some joint conditions
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Rectal bleeding, acute abdominal conditions, pregnancy.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): A two-step approach: preparing waste material (munzij) with herbal drinks, then expelling it (mushil) with a mild purgative.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: You take herbal preparations over several days, then a purgative under supervision.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Skin conditions, joint and digestive complaints
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Pregnancy, weakness, dehydration; supervision needed.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Specific foods and physical exercise recommended by the doctor according to your temperament.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Meals and an exercise plan are prescribed; some hospitals provide these.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Digestion, weight, general health
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Follow your doctor's advice if you have diabetes, kidney or heart disease.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: General diet and exercise benefits accepted

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Unani herbal, mineral and animal-origin medicines prescribed after assessment.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: You get a consultation and take prepared medicines; NIUM provides free medicine to IPD patients per its hospital services.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Chronic skin, digestive, respiratory, joint conditions
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Mineral or metal-containing preparations need strict quality testing; mention all medicines you take.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Limited; some individual herbs studied

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): A Siddha therapy using gentle pressure and manipulation on specific points to relieve pain and restore movement, often combined with oils.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: A therapist presses and manipulates points for 20-45 minutes; hospitals such as NIS and SCRI offer Varmam in OPD and IPD.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Back pain, disc problems, cervical and lumbar spondylosis, joint pain, dislocations
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Fractures, severe injury, spinal cord problems; always get a medical diagnosis first.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Some case studies and small studies; limited

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): A Siddha massage using strokes and pressure, with herbal oils.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Therapist massages along the body for 30-60 minutes.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Muscle pain, joint stiffness, relaxation
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Skin infection, fever, acute injury.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Relaxation benefits accepted; others limited

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): A warm herbal paste or poultice applied to painful or swollen areas.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: A paste is spread over the area and covered for a period.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Joint pain, swelling, muscle ache
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Skin allergy, open wounds.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Application of heat through warm herbal pads or cloth to painful areas.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Warm herbal cloth pads are pressed on the area for about 20-30 minutes.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Joint and muscle pain, stiffness
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Fever, skin burns or infections, reduced skin sensation.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Herbal steam (Vethu) and medicated smoke or fumigation (Pugai) used for certain conditions.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Steam or smoke is applied in a controlled way under supervision.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Respiratory congestion, joint conditions, skin conditions
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Asthma or lung disease (smoke may irritate), pregnancy, heart disease.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Traditional use; little formal clinical evidence

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Prescribed herbal and, in some cases, mineral or metal-based preparations (such as 'chenduram' or 'parpam').
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Prescribed after consultation; hospitals source medicines from state-run suppliers per NIS.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Skin conditions (e.g. psoriasis at SCRI), diabetes, joint conditions
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Metal or mineral preparations should only come from tested, reputable sources due to heavy-metal contamination risk (see Safety Notes).
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Limited; research ongoing at institutes

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Yoga and breathing practices linked to the Siddha tradition; NIS has a dedicated department and a yoga OPD.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: A therapist teaches practices as part of treatment.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Stress, lifestyle conditions, general wellbeing
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: As for other yoga practices.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Limited

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): A long consultation covering symptoms, lifestyle, emotions and history, used to choose a remedy.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: You answer detailed questions for 30-60 minutes; the doctor decides on a remedy and dose.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Used to select remedies for chronic and acute complaints
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Do not delay urgent medical care or stop prescribed medicines because of homeopathic treatment.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Consultation itself is accepted; see remedies below
Treatment Guide.Typically offered at: NIH Kolkata, Dr Batra's and others

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Remedies made from plant, mineral or animal substances that are diluted and shaken in stages. Many are diluted so far that no original substance remains.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: You take small pills or liquid drops as directed.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Chronic complaints, allergies, skin conditions, stress
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: Generally safe because of dilution, but should not replace proven treatment for serious or urgent conditions.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: Major reviews (e.g. Australia's NHMRC 2015) found no reliable evidence of effectiveness beyond placebo for the conditions studied; evidence is contested by supporters

Treatment Guide.What it is (plain English): Treating the whole person - physical symptoms, personality and emotions - rather than one symptom.
Treatment Guide.What happens in a session: Follow-up visits every few weeks to adjust remedies.
Treatment Guide.Traditionally used for (benefits): Long-standing complaints; general wellbeing
Treatment Guide.Who should avoid it / cautions: As above; keep your regular doctor informed.
Treatment Guide.Evidence note: As above

Safety Notes.Topic: Heavy metals in some Ayurvedic medicines
Safety Notes.What to know: A study of Ayurvedic medicines sold online found about one in five of those tested contained detectable lead, mercury or arsenic (US- and Indian-made alike). Regulators in the US, Australia and New Zealand have issued warnings. Risks are higher for mineral or metal preparations (rasa shastra) and for pregnant women and children.
Safety Notes.Suggested action on your platform: Use only medicines from accredited hospitals or licensed, tested manufacturers. Ask for ingredient lists and batch/test information. Do not buy unlabelled remedies online or from street sellers.
Safety Notes.Source: JAMA 2008 (Saper et al.); NC DHHS; FDA; Medsafe NZ (2025); Victorian Dept. of Health

Safety Notes.What to know: Some countries restrict or ban importing Ayurvedic or traditional medicines. For example, Australian health authorities advise avoiding Ayurvedic products that lack an AUST R or AUST L registration number.
Safety Notes.Suggested action on your platform: Tell guests to check their own country's customs and medicine rules before buying medicines to take home.
Safety Notes.Source: Victorian Dept. of Health via Pharmacy Daily (2025)

Safety Notes.What to know: Many Ayurvedic herbs and formulas are not proven safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding, and some therapies (induced vomiting, purgation, enemas, bloodletting, strong heat) are unsuitable.
Safety Notes.Suggested action on your platform: Show a clear 'consult your doctor first' notice for pregnant or breastfeeding guests and for children's treatment.
Safety Notes.Source: Herb and supplement monograph; Dr Weil site

Safety Notes.What to know: Detox therapies can cause dehydration, blood-pressure changes and electrolyte shifts. People with heart, kidney, liver disease, diabetes or on blood thinners need medical clearance, and herbs can interact with medicines.
Safety Notes.Suggested action on your platform: Include a medical questionnaire in your booking flow and ask guests to bring a doctor's letter and current medicine list.

Safety Notes.Topic: Not a substitute for emergency or standard care
Safety Notes.What to know: AYUSH therapies should not replace urgent care for serious conditions such as heart attack, stroke, cancer, severe infection or injury. Reports on Panchakarma and similar therapies note they must be given by qualified physicians.
Safety Notes.Suggested action on your platform: Display a plain-language disclaimer on every treatment page and encourage guests to keep their regular doctors informed.

Safety Notes.What to know: Evidence varies widely: yoga has reasonable evidence for stress and back pain; many Ayurvedic, Unani and Siddha therapies have limited or mixed evidence; homeopathic remedies have not shown reliable effectiveness beyond placebo in major reviews. 'Traditionally used for' wording is more accurate than 'cures'.
Safety Notes.Suggested action on your platform: Avoid words like 'cure' or guaranteed outcomes. Keep the Evidence note column visible on treatment pages to protect guests and your platform.
Safety Notes.Source: Compiled from reviews cited in the Evidence note column

Safety Notes.What to know: Bloodletting, cupping with incisions, and leech therapy carry infection and bleeding risks if equipment is not sterile.
Safety Notes.Suggested action on your platform: Only list providers who confirm sterile single-use equipment, and fresh leeches used once on one patient.

Safety Notes.What to know: Ayurveda hospitals can be checked on the NABH accredited AYUSH hospitals list. Yoga schools can be checked on Yoga Alliance and government affiliation. Retreats listed on aggregators are not necessarily medically supervised.
Safety Notes.Suggested action on your platform: Mark each listing as 'clinical (hospital)' or 'wellness retreat', as in the Institutions sheet.
